{{Short description|Concept in mathematics}}
{{Lie groups |Classical}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''special linear Lie algebra''' of order <math>n</math> over a [[field (mathematics)|field]] <math>F</math>, denoted <math>\mathfrak{sl}_n F</math> or <math>\mathfrak{sl}(n, F)</math>, is the [[Lie algebra]] of all the <math>n \times n</math> [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] (with entries in <math>F</math>) with [[trace (linear algebra)|trace]] zero and with the [[Lie algebra|Lie bracket]] <math>[X,Y] := XY-YX</math> given by the [[Commutator#Ring theory|commutator]]. This algebra is well studied and understood, and is often used as a model for the study of other Lie algebras.  The [[Lie group]] that it generates is the [[special linear group]].

==Applications==
The Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C}</math> is central to the study of [[special relativity]], [[general relativity]] and [[supersymmetry]]: its [[fundamental representation]] is the so-called [[spinor representation]], while its [[adjoint endomorphism|adjoint representation]] generates the [[Lorentz group]] SO(3,1) of special relativity.

The algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{R}</math> plays an important role in the study of [[chaos theory|chaos]] and [[fractal]]s, as it generates the [[Möbius group]] [[SL(2,R)|SL(2,'''R''')]], which describes the [[automorphism]]s of the [[Hyperbolic geometry#Models of the hyperbolic plane|hyperbolic plane]], the simplest [[Riemann surface]] of negative curvature; by contrast, [[SL(2,C)|SL(2,'''C''')]] describes the automorphisms of the hyperbolic {{nowrap|3-dimensional}} ball.

== Representation theory ==
{{see also|Representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras}}
=== Representation theory of sl<sub>2</sub>C ===

The Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C}</math> is a three-dimensional [[complex number|complex]] Lie algebra. Its defining feature is that it contains a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] <math>e, h, f</math> satisfying the commutation relations
:<math>[e,f]=h</math>, <math>[h,f]=-2f</math>, and <math>[h,e]=2e</math>.
This is a [[Cartan-Weyl basis]] for <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C}</math>.
It has an explicit realization in terms of 2-by-2 complex matrices with zero trace:

:<math>E = \begin{bmatrix}
0&1\\
0&0
\end{bmatrix}
</math>, <math>F = \begin{bmatrix}
0&0\\
1&0
\end{bmatrix}
</math>, <math>H = \begin{bmatrix}
1&0\\
0&-1
\end{bmatrix}
</math>.

This is the [[fundamental representation|fundamental]] or defining representation for <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C}</math>.

The Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C}</math> can be viewed as a [[linear subspace|subspace]] of its [[universal enveloping algebra]] <math>U = U(\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C})</math> and, in <math>U</math>, there are the following commutator relations shown by [[mathematical induction|induction]]:<ref name=Kac>{{harvnb|Kac|1990|loc=§ 3.2, pp 30–31.}}</ref>
:<math>[h, f^k] = -2 k f^k, \, [h, e^k] = 2 k e^k</math>,
:<math>[e, f^k] = -k(k - 1)f^{k-1} + k f^{k-1} h</math>.

Note that, here, the powers <math>f^k</math>, etc. refer to powers as elements of the algebra ''U'' and not matrix powers. The first basic fact (that follows from the above commutator relations) is:<ref name=Kac /> {{math theorem|name=Lemma|math_statement=Let <math>V</math> be a [[representation of a Lie algebra|representation]] of <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C}</math> and <math>v</math> a vector in it. Set <math>v_j = {1 \over j!} f^j \cdot v</math> for each <math>j = 0, 1, \dots</math>. If <math>v</math> is an [[eigenvector]] of the action of <math>h</math>; i.e., <math>h \cdot v = \lambda v</math> for some complex number <math>\lambda</math>, then, for each <math>j = 0, 1, \dots</math>,
*<math>h \cdot v_j = (\lambda - 2j) v_j</math>.
*<math>e \cdot v_j = {1 \over j!} f^j \cdot e \cdot v + (\lambda - j + 1) v_{j-1}</math>.
*<math>f \cdot v_j = (j+1) v_{j+1}</math>.
}}

From this [[lemma (mathematics)|lemma]], one deduces the following fundamental result:<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|2001|loc=Ch IV, § 3, Theorem 1. Corollary 1.}}</ref>

{{math theorem|name=Theorem|math_statement=Let <math>V</math> be a representation of <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C}</math> that may have infinite dimension and <math>v</math> a vector in <math>V</math> that is a <math>\mathfrak{b} = \mathbb{C} h + \mathbb{C} e</math>-weight vector (<math>\mathfrak{b}</math> is a [[Borel subalgebra]]).<ref>Such a <math>v</math> is also commonly called a primitive element of <math>V</math>.</ref> Then
*Those <math>v_j</math>'s that are nonzero are [[linearly independent]].
*If some <math>v_j</math> is zero, then the <math>h</math>-[[eigenvalue]] of ''v'' is a nonnegative [[integer]] <math>N \ge 0</math> such that <math>v_0, v_1, \dots, v_N</math> are nonzero and <math>v_{N+1} = v_{N+2} = \cdots = 0</math>. Moreover, the subspace spanned by the <math>v_j</math>'s is an irreducible <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2 \mathbb{C}</math>-subrepresentation of <math>V</math>.}}

The first statement is true since either <math>v_j</math> is zero or has <math>h</math>-eigenvalue distinct from the eigenvalues of the others that are nonzero. Saying <math>v</math> is a <math>\mathfrak{b}</math>-weight vector is equivalent to saying that it is simultaneously an eigenvector of <math>h</math> and <math>e</math>; a short calculation then shows that, in that case, the <math>e</math>-eigenvalue of <math>v</math> is zero: <math>e \cdot v = 0</math>. Thus, for some integer <math>N \ge 0</math>, <math>v_N \ne 0, v_{N+1} = v_{N+2} = \cdots = 0</math> and in particular, by the early lemma,
:<math>0 = e \cdot v_{N+1} = (\lambda - (N+1) + 1) v_N,</math>
which implies that <math>\lambda = N</math>. It remains to show <math>W = \operatorname{span} \{v_j \mid j \ge 0\}</math> is irreducible. If <math>0 \ne W' \subset W</math> is a subrepresentation, then it admits an eigenvector, which must have eigenvalue of the form <math>N - 2j</math>; thus is proportional to <math>v_j</math>. By the preceding lemma, we have <math>v = v_0</math> is in <math>W</math> and thus <math>W' = W</math>. <math>\square</math>

As a [[corollary]], one deduces:
*If <math>V</math> has finite dimension and is irreducible, then <math>h</math>-eigenvalue of ''v'' is a nonnegative integer <math>N</math> and <math>V</math> has a basis <math>v, f v, f^2 v, \cdots, f^N v</math>.
*[[Converse (logic)|Converse]]ly, if the <math>h</math>-eigenvalue of <math>v</math> is a nonnegative integer and <math>V</math> is irreducible, then <math>V</math> has a basis <math>v, f v, f^2 v, \cdots, f^N v</math>; in particular has finite dimension.

The beautiful special case of <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2</math> shows a general way to find irreducible representations of Lie algebras. Namely, we divide the algebra to three subalgebras "h" (the [[Cartan algebra|Cartan subalgebra]]), "e", and "f", which behave approximately like their namesakes in <math>\mathfrak{sl}_2</math>. Namely, in an irreducible representation, we have a "highest" eigenvector of "h", on which "e" acts by zero. The basis of the irreducible representation is generated by the action of "f" on the highest eigenvectors of "h". See the [[theorem of the highest weight]].

=== Representation theory of sl<sub>''n''</sub>C ===
{{expand section|date=September 2020}}
When <math>\mathfrak g = \mathfrak{sl}_n \mathbb C = \operatorname{\mathfrak{sl}}V</math> for a complex vector space <math>V</math> of dimension <math>n</math>, each finite-dimensional irreducible representation of <math>\mathfrak g</math> can be found as a subrepresentation of a [[tensor product of representations|tensor power]] of <math>V</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Serre|2001|loc=Ch. VII, § 6.}}</ref> 

The Lie algebra can be explicitly realized as a matrix Lie algebra of traceless <math>n\times n</math> matrices. This is the fundamental representation for <math>\mathfrak{sl}_n \mathbb{C}</math>. 

Set <math>M_{i,j}</math> to be the matrix with one in the <math>i,j</math> entry and zeroes everywhere else. Then
:<math>H_i := M_{i,i} - M_{i+1,i+1},\text{ with } 1 \leq i \leq n-1</math>
:<math>M_{i,j},\text{ with } i \neq j</math>
Form a basis for <math>\mathfrak{sl}_n \mathbb{C}</math>. This is technically an abuse of notation, and these are really the image of the basis of <math>\mathfrak{sl}_n \mathbb{C}</math> in the fundamental representation.

Furthermore, this is in fact a Cartan–Weyl basis, with the <math>H_i</math> spanning the Cartan subalgebra. Introducing notation <math>E_{i,j} = M_{i,j}</math> if <math>j > i</math>, and <math>F_{i,j} = M_{i,j}^T = M_{j,i}</math>, also if <math>j > i</math>, the <math>E_{i,j}</math> are positive roots and <math>F_{i,j}</math> are corresponding negative roots.

A basis of  [[Root system#Positive roots and simple roots|simple roots]] is given by <math>E_{i,i+1}</math> for <math>1 \leq i \leq n-1</math>.
